# LP2-31: periodic IoC for periods 2–20

**Computationally checked; human review pending.** Codex reran the script and reviewed the separate position-pair oracle on 20 October 2026. This is a bounded statistical result, not a decipherment or a human-reviewed conclusion.

## Question

Does LP2-31 have an unusually large within-column coincidence score at any period from 2 through 20, relative to random reorderings of the same rune multiset?

This is a test of one ordering statistic. It does not attempt decryption or determine whether the page uses Vigenère.

## Scope fixed before the first run

The plan is in `plan.json`, committed as `e515465` before computing the first result. It selects LP2-31, periods 2–20 inclusive, offset zero, 999 shuffles, seed 330131 and a 0.05 threshold. These are declared choices for this run, not a claim that the question or page was selected independently of all prior research.

The input is the complete archived rune stream, including headings. Remove every character outside the 29-rune alphabet before assigning positions. No corrections, decryption, region selection or cross-page concatenation are applied. The resulting length is 269 runes. Input paths and SHA-256 hashes are in `record.json` and `results.json`.

## Method

For period k, put positions with the same remainder modulo k in the same column. Count matching ordered pairs in each column and add them. Divide by the total number of ordered pairs available within all columns:

```
pooled IoC(k) = sum over columns and symbols of n(c,s)*(n(c,s)-1)
                / sum over columns of N(c)*(N(c)-1)
```

This weights columns by their number of pairs; it is not the unweighted mean of column IoCs. No pairs between different columns count.

Take the maximum over all 19 periods. Shuffle the original rune list afresh for each trial, preserving its exact symbol counts. Repeat the entire 19-period scan on every shuffled version and retain that trial's maximum. Compare maxima to maxima, rather than comparing the selected observed peak with an unselected single-period null distribution.

The random generator is Python's `random.Random(330131)`, using `shuffle`. Exact rational comparisons include ties. The Monte Carlo value is:

```
(1 + number of shuffled maxima >= observed maximum) / (999 + 1)
```

All observed period scores are retained. Each shuffled trial stores all 19 numerators, aligned with the observed periods. Their denominators do not depend on rune order and are stored once in the observed rows. The trial maximum is also stored as an exact fraction.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, using Python 3.12.10 and its standard library:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/check.py
python experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/run.py --check
```

The independent check enumerates pairs of positions directly, instead of counting frequencies in columns. It checks a constant string, an alternating string, and every tested period of the actual page. The alternating control has pooled IoC 1 at period 2.

The full rerun compares every stored field, including all shuffle scores and input hashes. It should report exact reproduction and:

```
n: 269
best_periods: [13]
exceedances: 213
monte_carlo_p: 0.214
below_threshold: false
```

To save a separate report:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/run.py --output my-periodic-ioc.json
```

An existing output file is never overwritten. No network service, model, API key or third-party package is used. A changed input hash or random-generator behavior can prevent byte-for-byte reproduction; investigate rather than replacing the expected output automatically.

## Results

![Observed pooled IoC by period. The highest bar is period 13; the maximum-adjusted shuffle comparison is p = 0.214.](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/period-scan.svg)


Period 13 has the unique largest observed score: 216 / 5300 = 0.04075471698. Its columns contain 20 or 21 runes.

Of 999 random reorderings, 213 have a maximum at least this large somewhere in the same period range. The corrected Monte Carlo value is 214 / 1000 = 0.214. It is not below the declared 0.05 threshold.

For scale, the approximate Monte Carlo standard error of the estimated tail frequency is 0.013, using sqrt(q*(1-q)/999) with q = 213/999. This describes simulation uncertainty, not uncertainty about a cipher or plaintext. The reported Monte Carlo value has increments of 0.001.

## Interpretation and limitations

This run does not provide evidence, at the declared threshold, for singling out period 13 from this scan. It does not establish that LP2-31 lacks periodic structure. A cipher may produce structure that this statistic, input convention or period range does not detect.

The null model treats rune order as exchangeable conditional on its counts. It does not preserve word lengths, punctuation positions, local repeated patterns or possible region boundaries. Rejecting it would not prove any particular encryption method. Failing to reject it does not prove randomness.

The maximum comparison accounts for selecting among periods 2–20 in this run. It does not correct for choosing LP2-31, trying different text regions or previous unrelated tests. Periods outside the range, other pages, corrected streams, alternative statistics and actual key searches remain untested here.

No shift or Vigenère key is inferred. The period-13 peak is retained as a descriptive result, not promoted to a solution.

## Sources and related work

- [LP2-31 record and original-source links](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/page/lp2-31)
- [IoC definition, baseline and invariants](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/index-of-coincidence)
- [Reproducibility requirements](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/reproducibility)

The whole-page baseline does not test ordering: shuffling preserves global IoC. This experiment adds an order-sensitive column statistic and a declared shuffle comparison. No earlier experiment is imported as a completed run.

## Retest and changes after inspection

On 20 October 2026, the independent position-pair check passed, and all observed and simulated numerical fields reproduced exactly. The only difference from the first saved output was the SHA-256 of `data/index.json`, whose page metadata had since changed. The plan and rune input hashes were unchanged. No period range, threshold, seed, sample count, or scoring rule was changed.

The original report is preserved as [original output](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/results-original.json). The [current report](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/results.json) records the current input hash. The checked script reproduces the current report exactly, including all 999 trials. The [chart script](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/plot.py) reads that report without running another experiment.

This record is the baseline for the periodic-IoC shuffle family. Future variants must identify each changed scope field and give their own plan, output and interpretation. A [within-row shuffle variant](#/experiments/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc) now preserves each archived row’s length and rune counts while leaving the observed statistic unchanged. Human review is still pending; the computational review was performed by Codex, not by an independent human researcher.

# LP2-31 periodic IoC: preserving row composition

## Why change the null model?

The baseline shuffles all 269 runes together. That preserves the page's total counts but can move any rune to any row. If rows differ in composition, that comparison removes those differences as well as the ordering under investigation.

This variant instead preserves each archived row's length and exact rune counts, shuffling only within that row. It asks a conditional question about order after holding row composition fixed. This is not automatically a better model; it makes a different assumption visible.

LP2-31 has twelve ordinary text rows and no separately identified heading. No row was removed or renamed as a heading for this test. Archived transcription lines provide the boundaries.

## Plan and relation to the baseline

The plan and runner were committed as `8dfc7c0` before executing the variant. The variant was motivated after the whole-page result was known; it is not independent confirmation and does not account for selecting among null models.

Only the shuffle procedure changes. The input remains the same 269 runes, periods remain 2–20 inclusive, the statistic remains pooled within-column matching pairs, and each trial's maximum is compared with the observed maximum. There are still 999 trials, seed 330131, greater-than-or-equal ties, plus-one Monte Carlo correction, and a 0.05 threshold.

The twelve row lengths are:

```
23, 22, 24, 24, 22, 22, 21, 22, 21, 24, 22, 22
```

Remove non-alphabet characters inside each row, shuffle that row's runes, then concatenate rows in their original order. Column positions run across the concatenated page; they do not restart at row boundaries. The same seed does not make the two models' individual shuffled pages equivalent or create a paired statistical test.

## Results

| Quantity | Whole-page baseline | Within-row variant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input runes | 269 | 269 |
| Observed peak period | 13 | 13 |
| Observed peak fraction | 216/5300 | 216/5300 |
| Null maxima at least observed | 213/999 | 245/999 |
| Plus-one Monte Carlo p | 0.214 | 0.246 |
| Below declared 0.05 threshold | No | No |

The observed scores agree exactly for every period, as they should: the observed input and scoring procedure did not change. The within-row comparison is 246/1000 = 0.246. Its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is 0.014, using sqrt(q*(1-q)/999) with q=245/999. This describes simulation uncertainty, not confidence in a cipher.

The two runs give the same threshold decision under their different assumptions. The difference between 0.214 and 0.246 is not evaluated as a separate statistical effect, and neither p-value is the probability that period 13 is the true key length.

## Reproduce

From a repository checkout with Python 3.12.10:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/check.py
```

The runner compares every observed field and all 999 stored trial records. The separate checker verifies the twelve row lengths, exact agreement with the baseline's observed scores, and a position-pair oracle for all observed periods and the first three seeded null trials. That oracle directly enumerates position pairs rather than using column-frequency counts. The runner also asserts preservation of each row's multiset in every trial.

[Download the complete variant output](experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/results.json). All 19 period numerators are stored for every shuffle; the denominators are in the observed rows. The comparison diagram is generated from the two saved reports. Neither the checker nor the plot interprets candidate plaintext or calls an AI service.

## Retest and changes after inspection

Codex reran the complete variant and performed the separate checks on 20 October 2026. Every stored field reproduced. No null rule, period range, input boundary, seed, threshold or statistic changed after the variant's first result. The checker and comparison graphic were added afterward for verification and presentation. Human review remains pending.

## Interpretation and remaining limits

This row-conditioned null preserves more local composition than the whole-page null, but still discards within-row word boundaries and local patterns. It treats all rune permutations within a row as exchangeable. Neither model is a full model of a particular cipher or language.

This variant does not show that the page is random, that period 13 is impossible, or that Vigenère is absent. It also does not test different pages, period ranges, row selections, alternative statistics or key searches. Those changes must be documented separately rather than silently folded into this result.

# Fixed alphabet transformations and the warning opening

## Why test this?

A newcomer can reasonably try reusing the warning's Atbash method, shifting the rune alphabet, or reversing the text. These are small, finite searches. The difficult part is deciding what counts as success without picking an attractive fragment after looking at the output.

This test uses one deliberately narrow criterion: the first 12 decoded rune indices must equal the first 12 decoded runes of LP1-01's warning. The criterion is motivated by an existing reading, but there is no evidence that an unsolved page must repeat that opening. This is not an English detector.

## Plan and scope

The plan and runner were committed as `faab48f` before the first execution. All 56 archived pages LP2-00–55 are included, corresponding to their unsolved status in the source snapshot. This is not a claim about their present-day solving status.

For every page, keep all recognized runes, including headings, and remove other characters. Use indices 0–28. Try both original and whole-stream reversed order. For each order, evaluate both multipliers a = 1 and a = -1 with every additive offset b = 0–28, using `(a * index + b) % 29`.

The positive multiplier covers all constant shifts. The negative multiplier covers alphabet reversal with every shift; ordinary Atbash is a = -1, b = 28. The identity is included. Reversing a complete stream is not the same as reversing individual rows or words.

| Transformation class | Orders | Offsets | Pages | Cases | Exact matches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constant shift | 2 | 29 | 56 | 3248 | 0 |
| Reversed alphabet plus offset | 2 | 29 | 56 | 3248 | 0 |
| Total |  |  |  | 6496 | 0 |

These are parameter cases, not a promise that every resulting string is distinct.

## Result and interpretation

All 6496 cases completed. No output began with the specified 12-rune warning prefix. Every full candidate sequence is retained in the JSON output, not only its prefix or an attractive excerpt. Each case records the page, order, multiplier, offset, output indices, and exact-match flag.

This finding is negative only for the declared opening at position zero. It does not rule out meaningful text beginning differently, a heading that needs separate treatment, another region, or an arbitrary substitution. There is no significance estimate because this is an exhaustive exact-match query, not a statistical test of whether the text is English.

## Reproduce and inspect

Use Python 3.12.10 and the repository checkout:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-alphabet-warning-prefix/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-alphabet-warning-prefix/check.py
```

The first command regenerates and compares every candidate, input hash, and match flag. The second uses a separately constructed alphabet-walk lookup to verify all output indices and confirms that every parameter tuple is unique. It also checks the known warning's opening A,W,A against indices 24,7,24. Neither command uses a network service.

[Download all candidate outputs](experiments/records/lp2-alphabet-warning-prefix/results.json). To save a fresh report, run the runner with `--output my-prefix-scan.json`; it refuses to overwrite an existing file. Read `alphabet` to map output indices back to runes. Latin transliteration involves additional conventions and is not applied here.

## Retest and changes after inspection

Codex reran the complete scan and the separate oracle on 20 October 2026. All 6496 candidates reproduced exactly. No input-selection rule, prefix length, transformation, or stopping rule changed after the first result. The independent oracle was added after the first run as a verification step, not used to select results. Human review remains pending.

## Next variants

A different known opening, prefix position, heading convention, or transformation range must be declared as a new variant with the changes visible. Do not append extra guesses to this baseline and report only the final combined search. An exact match in any later variant would still require checking the rest of the page.

# Two known Vigenère keys against known openings

## Why this test?

Reusing a key that already worked elsewhere is an understandable first attempt. The known Welcome and second-koan readings supply two concrete key vectors. This experiment asks whether uninterrupted use of either vector recovers any of nine recorded openings at the beginning of an archived LP2-00–55 page.

It is an exact-opening search, not a general language test. There is no reason every valid plaintext must reuse one of these openings. A negative result therefore rules out only the declared combinations and criterion.

## Plan fixed before running

The plan and runner were committed as `8a93183` before execution. The selected input is the complete archived rune stream for each of LP2-00–55, including headings. Non-alphabet characters are removed. There are no corrections, reversals, interruptions or cross-page carry.

The two key vectors are copied from the published reading parameters, without re-encoding their labels as prime values:

| Known reading | Key indices | Phases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Welcome | 23, 10, 1, 10, 9, 10, 16, 26 | 0–7 |
| Second koan | 0, 10, 4, 0, 1, 19, 0, 18, 4, 18, 9, 0, 18 | 0–12 |

For each phase, both subtraction and addition are tested modulo 29. Each page starts independently at the selected phase. Every rune consumes one key value; punctuation consumes none. The known interruption lists are not transplanted onto unrelated pages, and there is no rule to skip every F.

This makes 42 parameter cases per page, or 2352 across 56 pages. These are parameter cases, not a claim that every output string is unique.

## Exact comparison

Each output's first 12 rune indices are compared with the first 12 indices from nine known-reading traces: Warning, Welcome, Some Wisdom, first koan, Loss of Divinity, second koan, Instruction, LP2-56 and LP2-57. The vectors, trace paths and hashes are fixed in the plan. Comparing rune indices avoids ambiguity from multi-letter Latin labels.

Each of the 2352 candidates receives nine exact comparisons: 21,168 in total. Nothing is searched at later positions. The criterion does not ask whether a candidate resembles English, has familiar short fragments, or scores well under a language model.

## Results

All 2352 cases completed, and no candidate matched any of the nine specified opening vectors. Every complete candidate sequence is retained, including its page, key ID, phase, arithmetic sign, and list of matching opening IDs. The list is empty for every case in this run.

This is not evidence that repeating keys cannot work on these pages. Different keys, interruption schedules, headings, beginnings, or page boundaries remain outside the test. It does not estimate a probability that any cipher hypothesis is true.

## Controls and independent check

The 17 known page readings reproduced before the search. Those controls use their own recorded boundary and interruption conventions; they are not counted among the 2352 unknown-page candidates.

The new decoder also recovers the first 12 known output indices of both Welcome and the second koan at phase zero with subtraction. Neither control has an interruption in those first 12 positions. This checks the same uninterrupted operation used in the new search.

A separate checker verifies every candidate using a rotated key iterator and explicit wraparound arithmetic, checks all nine opening vectors against the trace CSVs, and checks that every parameter tuple occurs exactly once. The complete runner was then repeated and every saved candidate and match decision agreed.

## Reproduce

Use Python 3.12.10 and a repository checkout. No third-party package, network connection or AI service is used.

```
python experiments/records/lp2-known-vigenere-keys/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-known-vigenere-keys/check.py
```

To save a separate report:

```
python experiments/records/lp2-known-vigenere-keys/run.py --output my-known-key-scan.json
```

The output file must not already exist. [Download the saved candidates](experiments/records/lp2-known-vigenere-keys/results.json). The `alphabet` field maps indices back to runes; `sign` is -1 for subtraction and +1 for addition. Phase is the first key slot consumed at the beginning of that page. This convention resets for every case.

## Retest and later changes

Codex performed the complete rerun and independent checker on 20 October 2026. No keys, phases, opening vectors, input rules or matching criteria changed after the first result. The checker and coverage diagram were added after the search to verify and explain the saved result. Human review remains pending.

## Related work and next variants

The [fixed-alphabet experiment](#/experiments/lp2-alphabet-warning-prefix) tests a different transformation family and a single warning prefix. Its result must not be added to this record as if the criteria were identical. The [Vigenère guide](#/wiki/vigenere) explains the known key use, and the [interruption guide](#/wiki/interruptions) explains why key alignment needs care.

A justified new key list, heading convention or interruption hypothesis needs a separately declared variant. An interruption search can grow rapidly; its bounds and stopping rule must be fixed before inspecting candidate text. Do not add exceptions merely until a fragment appears readable.

# Original JPEGs: default-key OutGuess retrieval

## Why run this?

Some known Liber Primus images contain messages recovered with OutGuess. A newcomer may reasonably try the same operation on the other images. This experiment records what that particular retrieval does, including failures and unverified output, instead of assuming that every byte stream is a message or every failure means an empty image.

## Plan fixed before execution

The runner and plan were committed as `8bca8ba` before the first run. The scope is all 75 archived manuscript JPEGs, plus the 2014 opening image and the compasses cover. Every original-image SHA-256 is fixed in the plan. Thumbnails, screenshots and recompressed images are excluded.

Each image receives exactly one invocation of OutGuess with retrieval mode and the literal key `Default key`. The timeout is 20 seconds per invocation. Ten expected payload hashes serve as positive controls. All output files, exit codes and stderr diagnostics are retained, including empty output files and abnormal exits. A second complete run checks reproducibility; it is not counted as 77 additional independent discoveries.

## Result

| Observed category | Images | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Known payload hash reproduced | 10 | Exact agreement with the archived extraction control |
| Nonempty output, exit code 0, no control | 21 | Unverified candidate bytes only |
| Retrieval rejected, exit code 1 | 5 | This retrieval did not succeed |
| Abnormal exit code 3221225620 | 41 | An unresolved failure of this tool/build on these inputs |
| Timeout | 0 | No invocation exceeded the declared time limit |

All 77 invocations were attempted. Ten controls matched. **The other 67 images are not established as free of hidden data.** The 21 candidate outputs are not authenticated messages, and the 41 abnormal exits prevent treating this as a clean image-wide negative result.

The repeated output length 58,152 occurs in 19 candidate records. It is a reported extraction length, not a discovered structure in the manuscript. The 21 candidate byte streams have distinct hashes. None contains the ASCII marker `-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----`; that limited observation neither validates nor rules out a different encoding or payload type. No signature verification or interpretation of candidate contents was performed in this experiment.

## How to reproduce

Use Python 3.12.10 and a locally available OutGuess executable. See the [OutGuess guide](#/wiki/outguess) for original-file selection and the known-payload controls.

```
python experiments/records/outguess-default-key/run.py --outguess outguess --output my-outguess-run
python experiments/records/outguess-default-key/check.py
```

The first command creates a new directory, refuses to reuse an existing one, and records your executable's SHA-256. Replace `outguess` with its full executable path if necessary. The second command audits the saved experiment: every image hash, output hash, expected control and record count. It does not run OutGuess.

To repeat the exact saved run with the same executable:

```
python experiments/records/outguess-default-key/run.py --outguess outguess --check
```

This checks the tool hash, all statuses, diagnostics and every saved payload byte. Paths to temporary files are normalized in diagnostics; diagnostic content is otherwise retained. A different binary or platform may legitimately produce different diagnostics or error behavior. Run it into a new directory and compare it as a build variant rather than replacing this baseline.

## Tool and build limitation

The recorded binary was a local Windows port of upstream commit `24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02`, built using MinGW-W64 GCC 16.1.0. Its SHA-256 is `b342b8b85d678d3b2ed26efab70fba2b3956725670be7149b89646868f0ebade`.

The existing build record describes use of the upstream allocation/read fallback instead of mmap, a compatibility byte-order helper, and binary-mode input on Windows. Matching the ten controls checks those particular extraction paths; it does not establish correct behavior on all other images. The 41 abnormal exits remain a substantial limitation. The executable is not included in the wiki downloads. A reader with a different build should preserve their new report as a comparison, not expect its executable hash to match.

## Retest and review

Codex ran the entire 77-image sweep twice on 20 October 2026. All return codes, normalized diagnostics and output bytes matched exactly. A separate saved-file audit checked all image and output hashes and the ten control comparisons. The original plan, key, timeout and image list did not change after the first run. The visual map was generated from the saved report; it does not run another extraction. Human review remains pending.

## What to test next

The most informative next variant is another documented OutGuess build on exactly the same files and key, focusing on whether the 41 abnormal exits persist. A new key is a different variable and should not be changed simultaneously if the purpose is to isolate build behavior. Other steganographic methods require their own clearly scoped experiment.
